title: Act I, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: At the feast of Lupercal a soothsayer warns Caesar to beware the ides of March; Caesar dismisses him. Cassius probes Brutus, who admits he fears the people will choose Caesar for king. Cassius tells how he saved Caesar from drowning and saw him sick with fever, and argues 'the fault... is not in our stars, but in ourselves.' Caesar tells Antony he distrusts Cassius's 'lean and hungry look.' Casca reports that Caesar refused a crown offered three times by Antony and then fell in a fit. Alone, Cassius plans to throw forged letters in Brutus's window.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act I, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of Cassius works on Brutus. writingPrompts.label: College Freshman

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore

Argue how the scene's handling of Cassius works on Brutus follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene II and its treatment of Cassius works on Brutus. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about Cassius works on Brutus in Julius Caesar. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Cassius works on Brutus. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Julius Caesar.

satQuestions.passage: Marry, before he fell down, when he perceived the common herd was glad he refused the crown, he plucked me ope his doublet and offered them his throat to cut. An I had been a man of any occupation, if I would not have taken him at a word, I would I might go to hell among the rogues. And so he fell. When he came to himself again, he said, If he had done or said anything amiss, he desired their worships to think it was his infirmity. Three or four wenches, where I stood, cried “Alas, good soul!” and forgave him with all their hearts: but there’s no heed to be taken of them: if Caesar had stabbed their mothers, they would have done no less.

literaryElements.label: Characterization
literaryElements.explanation: Cassius works on Brutus through flattery, envy and appeals to Roman honour; Brutus admits he fears "the people / Choose Caesar for their king." Caesar, observed close up, is deaf in one ear and suspicious of "lean and hungry" Cassius.

literaryElements.label: Dramatic irony
literaryElements.explanation: Offstage shouts (Caesar refusing the crown three times) punctuate the persuasion; Casca's mocking report undercuts Caesar's show of modesty.

literaryElements.label: Rhetoric
literaryElements.explanation: Cassius uses anecdote (Caesar drowning in the Tiber, shaking with fever) to make Caesar seem merely human.

themesAndDevelopment.development: Cassius argues that men, not fate, make their own subjection.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
